title: AI services
header: Expects an AI policy, referenced with extended-matching. Must precede the general proxy classification.

extended-matching is not optional here. Clients that run their own encrypted DNS never ask the gateway to resolve, so they arrive as a raw IP with an SNI, and claude.com in particular resolves to GFW poisoned addresses on those clients. extended-matching matches on the SNI and hands the connection to the policy to resolve again, which replaces the destination rather than only changing the route. Without it those clients connect to a poisoned address and hang.
This file owns the AI category outright. The plain GitHub API is not a model endpoint, while dedicated inference and agent services need an AI policy.

Scope: a service earns a line when it is an unambiguous AI product endpoint, meaning inference, chat, generation, or the agent tooling built on them. Benchmark sites, observability dashboards and vendor marketing stay out. An omission costs the ability to steer AI separately and to account for it as a category in the console, never connectivity, because everything else still lands on a proxy one way or another.
Chinese providers live in AI/AIChina.list on the domestic path.

title: Chinese AI services
header: Expects a mainland policy.

The mainland providers, kept apart from AI/AI.list so they never take the foreign exit and never depend on GEOIP to stay home. askdiandian.com is Xiaohongshu's AI search app, and jimeng.jianying.com is ByteDance's image and video generation site.

title: Apple Intelligence
header: Expects an AI policy, referenced with extended-matching. Must precede Platforms/Apple.list, which would otherwise route these direct like ordinary Apple services, by name and by address.

Private Cloud Compute reaches Apple's inference through these relay hosts, which are fronted by Cloudflare and Fastly rather than by Apple. The feature is region gated, so it needs the same foreign exit as every other AI service, which is why it is grouped with AI rather than with push and content.
gspe1-ssl.ls.apple.com answers the GeoServices country lookup that the eligibility check reads, so it takes the same exit as the relays.

apple-relay.apple.com shares 17.248.152.0/24 and 17.248.163.0/24 with the Private Relay ingress at mask.icloud.com and with the iCloud content edges, so the three can only be told apart by name; Platforms/Apple.list carries the address space for the flows that arrive without one, and sits behind this file so an address never outranks the name.

title: Apple push
header: Expects DIRECT. Lives in the overlay so push stays direct whatever policy the profile puts the company-wide Platforms/Apple.list on, and precedes the two Apple sets that leave the direct path.

APNs uses long-lived TCP connections, and instant delivery depends on them staying up. Every reselection of a proxy policy group severs those connections. iOS reconnects aggressively and can fall back to cellular, while macOS may back off exponentially and delay push delivery. DIRECT avoids proxy group reselection.
Push is reachable on the domestic path, so it stays DIRECT.
The egress region also influences which courier Apple assigns. A Hong Kong exit can assign us-courier.push.apple.com, sending notifications through a US courier.
IP ranges are Apple's published list: https://support.apple.com/en-us/102266

title: iCloud content
header: Expects DIRECT. Lives in the overlay so the content plane stays direct whatever policy the profile puts the company-wide Platforms/Apple.list on.

The MMCS content service carries iMessage attachments, Photos, Drive and Backup. On a proxy path, the profile's QUIC block rejects HTTP/3 handshakes, and TCP fallbacks inherit that path's instability.

The profile refuses QUIC to these names ahead of this file, so transfers arrive here over TCP. Direct QUIC can remain connected while transferring slowly, preventing a TCP fallback. The guard is a logical rule that takes this file as a sub-rule and matches names only; config/Surge/README.md explains why it never matches by address.

This file carries names only. The content edges are also reached with no SNI the gateway can read, and those flows can only match by address: Platforms/Apple.list carries Apple's address space for them, after the named exceptions, because an address rule would otherwise take a flow that arrived by address with an SNI the exceptions own.

title: GitHub
header: Expects a proxy policy, the same one as general traffic. The list keeps every GitHub host on that one policy: the release asset and Copilot blob hosts sit on S3 and Azure, inside the suffixes of Platforms/Amazon.list and Platforms/Microsoft.list, whose groups are chosen independently, and ghcr.io and formulae.brew.sh fail on the direct path. Must precede those sets.

Hong Kong exits can intermittently drop the TLS handshake to GitHub's Asia frontend (20.205.243.166). The client hello goes out and nothing returns until a browser retry succeeds. A group's availability probe may miss intermittent failures, so an exit outside Hong Kong is appropriate if this occurs.
ghcr.io lives here rather than in Registries/Registries.list: it is blocked on the direct path, and it is GitHub, so it should share their exit.

formulae.brew.sh is a GitHub Pages custom domain (CNAME homebrew.github.io) whose large indexes stall on the direct path. It belongs here rather than with brew.sh and docs.brew.sh or with Registries/Registries.list. brew.sh and docs.brew.sh reach a proxy through FINAL.
github.io is deliberately absent. GitHub Pages uses different infrastructure; the Pages custom domain above needs its own rule.

The two address rules cover clients that dial GitHub without a name: 20.205.243.0/24 is the Asia frontend and 185.199.108.0/22 serves githubusercontent.com as well as Pages. They carry no-resolve, so a Pages custom domain that arrives by name is still not matched here.

title: Cloudflare Tunnel
header: Expects DIRECT.
cloudflared dials the Cloudflare edge on 7844 and carries its own transport security. Proxying it adds a hop to every tunnelled service for no benefit.
cfargotunnel.com is the current connector hostname. argotunnel.com is the older name still in use on some agents. trycloudflare.com is the quick-tunnel front.

The connector dials the edge by address, so its QUIC transport arrives without a name and misses the suffixes above. 198.41.192.0/24 and 198.41.200.0/24 are Cloudflare edge ranges; proxying these connections can break the tunnel.

title: official package registries
header: Expects a proxy policy.

A generic download set mixes domestic mirrors, GitHub Pages indexes that stall on the direct path, and destinations the GFW blocks. This file owns the official registries so their policy is explicit. Blocked destinations such as gcr.io, pkg.dev, mega.nz and archive.org stay unclassified so FINAL carries them to a proxy.
Policy is a proxy because the direct path from the mainland answers slowly and can time out, which package managers feel on every metadata request.

Scope: the package body or index host of an official registry, a Linux distribution's package archive, or a toolchain's official download host. Website, documentation, and static-asset hosts stay out and reach FINAL. GitHub-hosted registries stay in GitHub/GitHub.list. Chinese mirrors stay on the domestic path. Docker Hub stays in Library/Developer/Docker.list. NuGet stays in Library/Platforms/Microsoft.list.

title: Alibaba false positives
header: Expects a mainland policy. Must precede the blocking rule sets.

The reject set classifies Alibaba's security SDK, device fingerprint and device identifier endpoints as tracking, and Platforms/Alibaba.list cannot shield them because it follows the reject layer. Taobao treats a client that cannot reach them as an untrusted device: the app can refuse to load and report that the network is restricted.
Analytics stay blocked: adashx, the ut hosts, mmstat and loggw carry no verdict the apps depend on.

title: Better Stack false positives
header: Expects a proxy policy. Must precede the imported reject layer.

Log shipping to Better Stack ingests at s<source>.<cluster>.betterstackdata.com, and the reject set classifies the whole zone as telemetry. Blocking an ingestion host stops its source from receiving lines even when the shipping client reports no error.

title: Douyin false positives
header: Expects a mainland policy. Must precede the blocking rule sets.
The reject set's keyword matching also catches Douyin's app API hosts on -normal.zijieapi.com and its realtime push channel, which takes the app off the air rather than removing an ad.

These hosts filter on the TLS fingerprint, so a bare curl reset by the origin cannot establish that the reject layer blocked them. Check the matched rule or switch the reject policy to DIRECT and see whether the symptom clears.

title: Kuaishou false positives
header: Expects a mainland policy. Must precede the blocking rule sets.
Live streams pull from ks.pull.yximgs.com, which the reject set treats as PCDN infrastructure.

title: Meituan false positives
header: Expects a mainland policy. Must precede the blocking rule sets.
d.meituan.net serves in-app imagery and the reject set classifies it as ad infrastructure. Blocking the host leaves blank image tiles.

title: Tailscale coordination and admin
header: Expects a proxy policy.
The coordination server is not reliably reachable from CN, and the admin console is ordinary browser traffic that has no reason to be direct.

title: Tailscale direct
header: Expects DIRECT. Must follow Coordination.list.
The process rules cover a local Tailscale client that dials DERP relays by bare address and would otherwise reach the fallthrough proxy.

The DERP relays double as STUN servers, so proxying them makes Tailscale advertise the proxy's address as its own endpoint. That defeats NAT traversal and pins every peer to relay. The guard that enforces this for the STUN port is a logical rule and cannot live in a rule set, so it stays inline in the profile:
AND,((PROTOCOL,UDP),(DEST-PORT,3478)),DIRECT

Only the DERP relay names are pinned here. The website and pkgs.tailscale.com are ordinary HTTPS that is slow on the direct path, so they reach a proxy through FINAL; log.tailscale.com is telemetry and lives in Library/Reject/Telemetry.list.

title: tailnet address space
header: Expects DIRECT on macOS and a Tailscale policy on iOS. Referenced twice, once per platform, with a different policy each time. On macOS the native client owns this range outside Surge's virtual interface, so it expects DIRECT. On iOS the tunnel runs inside Surge as a Tailscale policy, because iOS allows only one VPN tunnel and installing the official client would displace Surge entirely.
The platform split cannot live inside this file: rule set files have no platform directive. Reference it twice instead, and let the profile generator resolve the directives.

title: Ads
header: Expects a reject policy.
Known advertising hosts. Keep Rescue ahead of this file. Analytics and crash reporters stay out. Hang this on a policy that can be switched off rather than a hard REJECT.

title: HTTP DNS
header: Expects a reject policy.

Stops mainland apps from bypassing the gateway resolver. Hang this on a policy that can be switched off rather than a hard REJECT. If an app fails closed instead of falling back, that host belongs in Rescue.
DNSPod's public DoH under doh.pub and dns.pub is the same bypass with a general resolver behind it. The foreign public resolvers are in Proxy/DoH.list.

title: Telemetry
header: Expects a reject policy.

Usage telemetry, product analytics and crash reports that the imported reject layer lets through, so they would otherwise ride a proxy exit. Developer CLIs are the heaviest senders: they report on every command. Hang this on a policy that can be switched off rather than a hard REJECT.

Scope: the ingestion host, never the vendor's dashboard or API, which keep their own file or FINAL. Feature flag services stay out, because a client that cannot fetch its flags changes behavior. Our own services stay in Developer/Owned.list. A host whose company list sits in the overlay, ahead of the reject block (GitHub, AI, Tailscale coordination), cannot be caught here.

blocks.note: Sentry ingestion, per region. sentry.io itself stays in Developer/Sentry.list.
Datadog log and browser intake. The us5 browser intake is its own registrable domain.
PostHog ingestion. posthog.com itself is the product site.

Tailscale's log service. Clients keep working without it.

title: Unresolvable names
header: Expects a reject policy.

Names that can never resolve: the special-use TLDs of RFC 2606 and RFC 6761, and names under a TLD that does not exist. Without a rule they reach FINAL and are dialed through a proxy exit that cannot resolve them either: test fixtures under .test, connectivity probes under .invalid, and app placeholders such as uc.cmd. Bind it to REJECT: nothing here works on any path.
example.com and its siblings stay out. They are reserved but resolve and answer.

title: China CDN
header: Expects DIRECT.
Mainland content hosts keep large objects on the local last mile. ctlcdn.cn and ctadns.cn are China Telecom CDN zones; NetEase Cloud Music streams through names such as m701.music.126.net.ctlcdn.cn.
volcgslb.com and vedcdnlb.com are Volcano Engine CDN zones used by NetEase Cloud Music under names such as music.126.net.volcgslb.com; tcdnos.com carries app and game update downloads.

title: Carrier services
header: Expects DIRECT.

Wi-Fi Calling ePDG endpoints. The IKEv2/IPsec tunnel must terminate at the carrier from the real access network; through a proxy exit it can fail registration or pin calls to the exit region. The hostname pattern sits in the profile's always-real-ip so the phone sees real addresses, which also means the tunnel reaches the gateway by bare address and this name rule never sees it. Inline UDP 500 and 4500 rules in the profile catch those packets; this file keeps name resolution on the same path.
Carrier apps. China Telecom's app and account plane live under 189.cn; the carrier answers its customers on the access network it runs.

Handset address space. A mainland mobile carrier can number a handset interface from US DoD and UK MoD blocks, and peer-to-peer apps such as UU Remote offer that address as a connection candidate. It is unreachable from outside the carrier, but a candidate that falls to FINAL is dialed through a proxy exit. Surge maps a UDP socket as a whole, so the policy its first packet picks also carries later packets to relay servers and the handset's public address. These blocks need a direct rule to keep the entire socket on the access network.

title: Certificate validation
header: Expects DIRECT.

OCSP responders and CRL and AIA hosts of public CAs. A revocation check sits on the critical path of its TLS handshake. These CAs serve responders from anycast networks with mainland reach; Google's pki.goog does not and stays out. Apple's own responders live in Platforms/Apple.list and Microsoft's in Platforms/MicrosoftCDN.list.

title: Downloads
header: Expects DIRECT.

Netdisk fronts, OS and game content CDNs, and update and object storage hosts that work on the direct path. Steam and Nintendo delivery hosts follow the same policy for game downloads. Microsoft delivery lives in Platforms/MicrosoftCDN.list.
The 1Password, iStat Menus and PopClip update hosts answer slowly on the direct path, so they reach a proxy through FINAL.

title: NTP
header: Expects DIRECT.
Time sync should not ride a proxy path. These names sit in the profile's always-real-ip, so packets reach the gateway by bare address and only the inline UDP 123 rule in the profile catches them.

title: Private names
header: Expects DIRECT.
Names that never leave the machine or the LAN.

title: iCloud Private Relay
header: Expects DIRECT, referenced with extended-matching. Must precede Platforms/Apple.list, which would otherwise swallow the mask hosts; it exists as its own file so the relay can be switched off for the whole network by pointing it at REJECT.

Private Relay negotiates its own QUIC transport to the relay edge. On a proxy policy that bootstrap is blocked by the profile's QUIC policy and incurs a retry before TCP fallback. DIRECT lets it negotiate for itself. The relay ingress shares 17.248.152.0/24 and 17.248.163.0/24 with the iCloud content edges; the profile's iCloud content guard refuses QUIC by name only, so relay traffic keeps its QUIC whether it arrives by name or by address. To disable Private Relay at the network, point this file at REJECT in the profile.

title: Syncthing
header: Expects DIRECT.

Global discovery and relays, plus local Syncthing clients by process name. Announcing through a proxy registers the exit address as the device's endpoint, which defeats direct peer connections the same way a proxied STUN answer would. Peers and relays are dialed by bare address, so the inline TCP 22000 and 22067 rules in the profile keep the transfers themselves direct; this file covers the lookups and the local process.

title: Banks, direct
header: Expects DIRECT. Must follow Bank/Proxy.list, which takes two Hong Kong arms out of their mainland parents' suffixes, and precede DOMAIN-SUFFIX,cn.

A bank ties a session to the address it sees, so each bank takes one path for its whole estate, decided by name. This file holds the banks whose path is the real access network. It expects DIRECT rather than a mainland policy, so routing mainland traffic through a proxy never moves a bank.

Mainland banks and UnionPay take one direct path by name because their apps call each other inside a session. GEOIP can split a bank's hosts when DNS has no answer or its addresses vary. Hua Xia Bank's site answers on the direct path and can fail through a proxy exit.

Bank of China (Hong Kong) needs DIRECT because a proxy provider can refuse bochk.com by name even when BOCHK accepts the exit address. bocgroup.com serves from the same addresses with BOCHK's certificate, and 202.127.168.0/21 is BOCHK's allocation (netname BOCHKAS), so traffic that arrives by address takes the same path.

ICBC Asia runs on its parent's mainland infrastructure: mobilehk.icbc.com.cn and icbc-asia.icbc.com.cn use mainland carrier space, and www.icbcasia.com resolves into China Mobile space, so it stays with its parent. The Hong Kong arms with their own Hong Kong infrastructure are in Bank/Proxy.list.

A bank's second zones belong here too. A name this file misses reaches its path only through DOMAIN-SUFFIX,cn or GEOIP, so a mainland policy pointed at a proxy, or a missing DNS answer, can move it off the direct path. This covers China Minsheng's creditcard.cmbc.cn, CITIC's tech.citic and cfhc.citic, Ping An's pingan.com and orangebank.com.cn, China Merchants' cc.cmbchina.cn, UnionPay International, and Ping An Bank's sdb.com.cn inherited from Shenzhen Development Bank.

blocks.note: Bank of China (Hong Kong). The proxy provider refuses it.
ICBC Asia, on its parent's mainland infrastructure. Its app hosts sit under icbc.com.cn below.

title: Banks, proxied
header: Expects a proxy policy. Must precede Bank/Direct.list, whose mainland suffixes would otherwise take CCB Asia and BoCom Hong Kong.

A bank ties a session to the address it sees, so each bank takes one path for its whole estate, decided by name. Hong Kong and foreign banks take the proxy. GEOIP can split them: mainland resolvers hand some bank edges a mainland or Alibaba anycast address, sending those direct while the rest of the bank takes the proxy.
Analytics hosts such as smetrics.sc.com, svc2.sc.com, omns.americanexpress.com and analytics.chase.com are rejected by the reject layer, which this file follows, and stay rejected.

Scope: Hong Kong retail and virtual banks, and foreign banks. A Hong Kong arm with its own Hong Kong infrastructure belongs here even when a host sits under its mainland parent's zone: CCB Asia's www.asia.ccb.com resolves into CCB's Hong Kong network (AS38475), and BoCom Hong Kong's hk.bankcomm.com into the same Hong Kong range as bankcomm.com.hk. AlipayHK is a Hong Kong stored value licensee and sits here with HSBC's PayMe. Card networks are not banks and stay unclassified.

blocks.note: Hong Kong retail banks. HSBC's PayMe lives on HSBC's own top-level domain.
Hong Kong arms of mainland banks that run their own Hong Kong infrastructure

title: Apple
header: Expects DIRECT, referenced with extended-matching. The company-wide floor: every Apple name and Apple's own address space. Must follow Apple/AppleIntelligence.list, Media/AppleMedia.list, Platforms/AppleChina.list and Direct/PrivateRelay.list, the four Apple sets whose policy differs; everything else Apple lands here instead of in FINAL.

DIRECT keeps Apple services on a stable domestic path. On a proxy path, the profile's QUIC block can time out HTTP/3 before TCP fallback, and some Apple frontends refuse foreign exits. setup.icloud.com bootstraps iCloud sessions, while init.itunes.apple.com bootstraps the App Store. The company floor also covers iMessage identity under ess.apple.com, Game Center, gsas.apple.com, unlinkability.apple.com, tether.edge.apple, the partitioned p*-buy.itunes.apple.com store hosts, and iCloud Mail on me.com.

The address rules carry traffic that arrives without a name. iCloud content can run over HTTP/3 to edge-*.hkhkg2.icloud-content.com without a readable SNI, so those requests reach the gateway as bare addresses and can otherwise fall to FINAL, where block-quic rejects them. 17.0.0.0/8 and the three IPv6 blocks are Apple allocations; they cover the content edges (17.248.152.0/24 and 17.248.163.0/24, shared with Private Relay ingress and the Intelligence relay), gateway addresses (17.248.216.0/24), and time servers. QUIC to content names meets the profile's name guard first, because direct QUIC can transfer slowly without falling back to TCP. That guard leaves address based CloudKit migrations alone. These address rules follow the named exceptions: no-resolve avoids resolving a named request solely for address matching, but a request arriving by address with an SNI is still matched by address.
The services that keep a foreign exit on purpose stay out: Apple Intelligence in the overlay, TV and News in Media/AppleMedia.list.

title: Apple China
header: Expects a mainland policy, referenced with extended-matching. Must precede Platforms/Apple.list, whose apple.com suffix would otherwise take the -cn location and Maps hosts. Those hosts carry the region inside a label (gspe19-cn-ssl, gsp10-ssl-cn), which a suffix rule cannot see, so the wildcard does that work.

The mainland operated estate includes iCloud on GCBD, the .cn store, and location, Maps and search endpoints for mainland clients. These endpoints can still answer through a proxy, hiding a routing mismatch.

title: Baidu
header: Expects a mainland policy.

title: ByteDance
header: Expects a mainland policy.

Douyin, Toutiao, Feishu, Volcano Engine and the e-commerce and mini-app estates. TikTok stays in Media/TikTok.list and expects a streaming policy. The content CDNs (douyincdn.com, douyinvod.com, byteimg.com, bytecdn.cn, pstatp.com) live in Direct/CDNChina.list. Rescue/Douyin.list precedes the reject layer for the app hosts it blocks.

title: China services
header: Expects a mainland policy.

Mainland services without a dedicated file: XGIMI, Coolapk, BOSS Zhipin, ifanr's IoT cloud, Cece and GF Securities. The owners of 300hu.com, dittocdn.com, ndcpp.com, sjxydc.com and i-ttg.net are unidentified; these hosts are classified by their mainland routing.

title: Google
header: Expects a proxy policy, referenced with extended-matching.

The overlay AI list must precede this file so Gemini, AI Studio and the .google AI products stay on the AI policy. YouTube has its own file. The mainland endpoints live in Platforms/GoogleChina.list and must precede this file.

title: Google China
header: Expects a mainland policy. Must precede Platforms/Google.list.

The endpoints Google serves for the mainland include the reCAPTCHA mirror, .cn API and static mirrors, and the -cn download redirector. recaptcha.net lets sites work without a foreign exit; the proxy path can block its QUIC attempts.
app-analytics-services.com is Firebase Analytics and answers from Google's mainland addresses, so it belongs on the mainland path.

title: Huawei
header: Expects a mainland policy.
Reject/HttpDNS.list precedes this file for the HTTP DNS hosts under dbankcloud.

title: JD
header: Expects a mainland policy.
The store, payments and JD Cloud. The image CDN 360buyimg.com lives in Direct/CDNChina.list.

title: Meituan
header: Expects a mainland policy.
Meituan and Dianping. Rescue/Meituan.list precedes the reject layer for the image host it blocks; this file carries the rest.

title: Meta
header: Expects a proxy policy.
The company remainder. Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp have their own files.

title: Microsoft
header: Expects DIRECT or a proxy policy, referenced with extended-matching.

Accounts, Office, Azure, Bing, Skype and the VS Code service plane. Update and download hosts live in Platforms/MicrosoftCDN.list and must precede this file, whose suffixes would otherwise take them. Xbox has its own file. msftconnecttest.com and msftncsi.com sit in the profile's always-real-ip, so their probes reach the gateway by address and never match here.

title: Microsoft CDN
header: Expects DIRECT.

Update, download, Office delivery and certificate validation hosts. Must precede Platforms/Microsoft.list, whose suffixes would otherwise take them. update.code.visualstudio.com carries the VS Code update check.

download.prss.microsoft.com is deliberately absent. Its mainland edges can cap each direct connection, so a completed request says nothing about download speed. The zone falls through to Platforms/Microsoft.list, where a proxy policy can avoid the direct path's cap.

title: NetEase
header: Expects a mainland policy.
Mail, games, Yunxin and the music CDN mirrors. NetEase Cloud Music itself is music.163.com under this file.

title: Pinduoduo
header: Expects a mainland policy.
The app, its web front yangkeduo.com and image and video hosts belong on the mainland path. The reject layer precedes this file and keeps tracking hosts under th.pinduoduo.com blocked.

title: Tencent
header: Expects a mainland policy.
WeChat has its own file, the QQ media brands live in Media/China.list, and qcloudcdn.com in Direct/CDNChina.list.

title: Trip.com
header: Expects a mainland policy.
Ctrip and its international brand share infrastructure, so both names take the same policy.

title: Xiaomi
header: Expects a mainland policy.
Phones, the ROM, the account plane and home devices. Mijia camera and peer relay traffic under mijia.tech belongs on the domestic path.

title: Alibaba CIDR
header: Expects a mainland policy.

Alibaba's anycast space is dialed by address without a name the gateway can read. The blocks are registered in the United States, so GEOIP,CN misses them and FINAL can send them abroad. Taobao can then see one session from a mainland address and a foreign data center, which its risk control may restrict.

155.102.0.0/16 and 163.181.0.0/16 are originated by Taobao's network, AS24429. 47.246.0.0/16 and 139.95.0.0/16 are anycast blocks inside Alibaba Cloud's AS45102 that its apps also dial by address. The rest of AS45102 is rented cloud capacity in foreign regions and stays out. Place below domain rules. Pair with Platforms/Alibaba.list.

title: LAN
header: Expects DIRECT.
Surge also ships RULE-SET,LAN. This copy exists so a profile can stay inside this library.
100.64.0.0/10 is omitted on purpose: Tailscale/Tailnet.list owns that range. All address rules carry no-resolve.

title: Telegram CIDR
header: Expects a proxy policy.
Telegram data-center prefixes, written here the same way Apple Push carries Apple's published courier ranges. Place below domain rules. Pair with Social/Telegram.list.

title: Download clients
header: Expects DIRECT.
Process names for common download clients. Keep large transfers off the proxy path.

title: Proxy cores
header: Expects DIRECT.
Prevents the gateway from proxying another proxy process on the same machine.
